meta.title: 2026 has been the most pivotal year in my career… and it's only March
meta.author: drs

comments.author: dzwdz
comments.text:
AI is now highly skilled at programming, and better than me at almost every programming task, with inhumanly-low defect rates. The remaining issues are mainly steering problems


...how about the unavoidable plagiarism risk?

But hey, it's uneconomical to not use the plagiarism machine! I therefore gotta change my job away from a company that seems to be doing just fine without the plagiarism machine "is years behind adopting AI" for one that embraces the risk of plagiarism head-first! Look, the plagiarism risk is small enough not to matter anyways, right? Who cares if we do a little plagiarism?

I'm glad there aren't any other ethical issues with this new, much more economical approach. Anthropic deserves your $350/mo for the hard work it did exploiting the unpaid labor of FOSS maintainers. Besides, they might've "worked proactively to deploy [their] models to the Department of War", but they wrote a nice article about how they don't want their AI to be used for fully autonomous weapons yet, so they're all good. The gains over local LLMs are so worth it.

I hate this fucking industry. People used to have a spine.

comments.author: dzwdz
comments.text:
Re-reading the article, I've realized I kinda missed the entire Quilt rewrite thing.

Quilt is licensed under the GPLv2. Chris used AI to generate a suite of tests, then he used another AI[1] to rewrite it "from scratch", using only the AI trained on a lot of GPLv2 code, presumably including Quilt itself. The result was released on Github under the Unlicense.

I wonder what sort of reasoning Quilt's original authors had for using GPLv2 rather than dedicating it to the public domain. Whatever, I'm sure it wasn't very important.

[1] I assume what is meant there is that they didn't share a context window, I don't see why using a different model/paying two AI companies would matter here.

comments.author: marginalia
comments.text:
If you phrase it as "I took a code base, ran it through a series of programs, and I got a new code base that does the same thing", it does seem pretty tenuous to argue that this is isn't copyright infringement when re-encoding a Disney Blue-Ray with ffmpeg is (i.e. taking a movie, running it through a series of programs, and then outputting a movie that looks the same).

The clean-room analogy only works so long as the AI models have personhood.

comments.author: nextos
comments.text:
I spoke with a well-known IP barrister, and he was also surprised that people happily consider using what he described as a "statistical mirror" has no strings attached. At the very least, it is something legally dubious from an IP perspective.

Clean-room implementation was devised to avoid IP contamination. LLMs are, in many ways, the opposite. They have been pre-trained with everything under the sun, including data that has been harvested in dubious ways, let alone blatant copyright infringement in case of books, as indicated by recent pre-court settlements.

comments.author: orib
comments.text: It also only works if you assume that the model was not trained on the code in question.

comments.author: mtset
comments.text:
There’s a huge, growing gap between open weight models and the frontier. Models you can run yourself are toys. In general, almost any AI product or service worth your attention costs money.


A genuine question, here, for anyone who is pro-AI and believes this: do you not see this as a serious danger? If we accept that:

a) open-weight models that individuals can run themselves are far behind the frontier models, and
b) frontier model development companies are likely to survive financially,

is there any outcome that isn't these companies essentially centralizing all wealth? There was a piece on NPR today about this, which I'll quote:


[TRISTAN] HARRIS: The only way they can justify the amount of money that's been invested into this AI industry is if they race to replace economic labor in the economy. That's the stated mission statement of OpenAI - is to be able to do everything that a human laborer can do. [...] They're not racing to augment and support human workers. They're racing to replace human workers. And what that will lead to is unprecedented levels of concentration and wealth and power because essentially, all the money in the economy - instead of being paid to individual laborers, you're going to pay five to 10 AI companies to do all of the work.


Is this, somehow, wrong? Or, if it's right, why do you find it acceptable?

comments.author: addison
comments.text:
Will these kitchens still need human chefs like me by the end of the decade?


Well, yes, because one cannot be an effective reviewer of code without actually understanding code. The best solution is often not the easiest one, but the most sustainable, and I see little evidence that LLMs are "sustainable" by effectively any metric.

comments.author: abnercoimbre
comments.text:
We read the same piece, right? From the beginning (emphasis mine):


There were multiple factors, but it’s not mere chance it coincides with these early months of the automation of software engineering.


He proceeds to incorporate language from the blog post. "My ex-company was years behind adopting AI." "But this new employer is at the frontier."

Indeed, throughout the essay Chris is pivoting in oddly the same ways Shumer was advising, after literally referencing his advice. The latter had widespread circulation at the time (read: MEGA viral.)

Call my take immaterial, sure, but not lazy.
